AnyGoal: On World Model Generalization
Beyond Expert Rollouts

Heejeong Nam  Divyat Mahajan  Quentin Le Lidec  Randall Balestriero  David Klindt Affiliation: 
Affiliation: Brown University  Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory  Mila, Université de Montréal  New York University 
Abstract

The goal of a world model is to capture the dynamics of an environment. This has the great appeal that it allows agents to plan and simulate a course of actions with the help of a world model. For these uses to be reliable, however, the learned dynamics must behave well beyond the specific state–action combinations observed in expert rollouts. Despite this, the relationship between data coverage, dynamics generalization, and downstream planning performance remains underexplored. We study this relationship through the lens of compositional generalization: can a world model recombine familiar state and action factors into valid dynamics? To answer this, we introduce AnyGoal, a benchmark of goal-shifted task variants built from widely used world-model environments, together with an open-source library. Each task is designed to be within reach of a world model that has learned the underlying dynamics: individual state factors and actions remain within their training support, but their combinations are underrepresented in expert trajectories. Across multiple environments and world-model families, we find that current models consistently exhibit failures under these recombinations. By examining dynamics and representation failures across model families, interaction regimes, and evaluation metrics, we study where current world models generalize and where challenges remain for goal-shifted prediction and planning. Together, this framework, benchmark, and analysis provide a basis for evaluating progress toward world models that generalize to new planning tasks.

 Website    Code

1 Introduction

A key goal of physical intelligence is the ability to plan and perform new tasks. Routine tasks, such as driving to work, can be automatized and executed without much cognitive effort. Yet novel tasks requires us to plan and simulate the consequences of our actions. World models (Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018; Maes et al., 2026b; Ivashkov et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2025) aim to learn action-conditioned dynamics of environment by predicting how the world evolves under actions rather than task-specific behavior (Sutton and Barto, 2018). Therefore, a good world model should not merely memorize behavioral biases present in the training distribution. However, in-distribution evaluation offers limited evidence of reusable dynamics. Figure 1 illustrates a simple but strong example of this caveat. In Push-T, the agent must push a block to a target pose, so expert rollouts strongly couple far-from-block states with actions that move the agent toward the block. A model trained on Push-T may therefore learn this rollout regularity rather than the action-conditioned effect of the supplied action, as reflected by the action-sensitivity plot in Fig. 1.When evaluated on Avoid-T, which requires avoiding the block using familiar 2D navigation, the model fails.

If the training data fully covered the relevant joint state–action space, then a model could in principle predict correctly on that support. However, such coverage is unrealistic in many control problems, especially when the relevant space is high-dimensional. First, offline datasets for world-model training are often collected from goal-directed policies that reach task-relevant states (Burda et al., 2019), which can introduce strong state–action correlations. One possible remedy is to mix data from multiple policies (Zhao et al., 2026). However, even with such mixtures, it can be difficult to determine whether the resulting dataset sufficiently covers the relevant state–action space, especially when the true reachable set is unknown. Even when a coverage gap is identified, collecting targeted rollouts to fill it can be difficult in offline settings. This makes it necessary to study generalization under incomplete coverage, rather than assuming that data scale alone will resolve the issue.

Generalization of world models has been studied to some extent. Closest to our setting, Hansen and Wang (2026) study hallucination detection and mitigation in world models, while we evaluate generalization in a statistically controlled space with explicit state-action support checks. Other OOD evaluations introduce states or factors outside the training support (Maes et al., 2026a; Wang et al., 2026; Li et al., 2025). Such settings are valuable for testing robustness to novel factors or extrapolation, but they may go beyond the generalization expected from a reusable dynamics model.

What remains missing is a systematic evaluation of the generalization that a good world model should support. First, we formalize this criterion as compositional generalization (Wiedemer et al., 2024b) and link it to goal shifts and behavior bias in the training data. We further show that the bias is empirically realized through targeted action interventions on familiar but under-covered state–action combinations, eliciting degenerate model responses. We then propose AnyGoal (Fig. 2), a benchmark of goal-shifted task variants built from widely used world-model environments. To remain in the compositional-generalization regime, AnyGoal preserves the observed marginal support of states, actions, task-relevant factors, and physical rules, while changing the joint combinations induced by the training behavior distribution and targeting under-covered state–action regions. With AnyGoal, we test whether current world models can generalize to new tasks without requiring extrapolation to unseen states, actions, or visual factors. Across this controlled setting, we observe broad failures across modeling paradigms, including generative world models (Zhu et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2026) and JEPA-style architectures (Maes et al., 2026b; Ivashkov et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2025). Our results then characterize this degradation across several axes, showing that failures can arise from both dynamics prediction and representation learning, and that their severity depends on task complexity, evaluation metric, and model family. Finally, we outline a theoretical direction toward compositional generalization for world models, framing what future models may need in order to move beyond behavior-biased rollouts.

2 Related Works

Compositional generalization diagnostics and benchmarks.

Compositional generalization tests whether a model can recombine familiar components into unseen configurations, a key challenge when possible compositions exceed finite data coverage. Early sequence-to-sequence benchmarks such as SCAN (Lake and Baroni, 2018) and CFQ (Keysers et al., 2020) exposed this failure mode through controlled compositional splits. The same diagnostic was subsequently adopted in vision and multimodal settings, with benchmarks such as CLEVR (Johnson et al., 2017), Winoground (Thrush et al., 2022), and CVR (Zerroug et al., 2022) testing whether familiar objects, attributes, and relations can be composed correctly. These failures remain prominent in modern large-scale models: ConceptMix (Wu et al., 2024) shows that text-to-image models degrade as prompts require more familiar concepts to be composed jointly, while recent vision–language work continues to reveal failures in object–attribute and relational composition (Assouel et al., 2026). At the same time, compositional evaluation is becoming broader and more systematic, with scalable protocols for probing generalization across controlled compositions (Camposampiero et al., 2026), and similar shifts being used as diagnostics in mechanistic interpretability (Pacela et al., 2026). AnyGoal brings this perspective to world models, where goal-directed trajectories naturally induce restricted joint coverage over otherwise familiar physical states and actions.

World-model generalization and support mismatch.

Recent world-model work has studied generalization through object-centric compositional dynamics (Zhao et al., 2022), composable causal components for unseen environments (Wang and Huang, 2025), multi-task world models (Georgiev et al., 2025), environment-level evaluation queries (Warrier et al., 2026), action-conditioned planning (Zhang and Du, 2026), and coverage-related hallucination failures (Hansen and Wang, 2026). However, less is known about whether expert-trained world models generalize to new goal-induced recombinations of familiar states and actions. This question is closely connected to support mismatch in offline reinforcement learning, where fixed behavior datasets can lead methods to fail when evaluating poorly covered state–action regions (Fujimoto et al., 2019; Kumar et al., 2019; Levine et al., 2020). Offline RL addresses support mismatch by constraining or regularizing policies toward covered regions (Gao et al., 2025b; Gao et al., 2025a; Laroche et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2025; Kumar et al., 2020; Tang et al., 2025). Model-based offline RL extends this issue to learned dynamics, motivating uncertainty- or pessimism-based objectives for poorly covered regions (Yu et al., 2020; Kidambi et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2021; Rigter et al., 2022). D4RL further shows that dataset composition strongly affects offline policy improvement (Fu et al., 2021). AnyGoal is complementary to these approaches: it evaluates whether the world model learns reusable dynamics under goal shifts.

3 Compositional Generalization for World Models

When should we say that a world model has learned reusable dynamics, rather than only the training behavior? In this section, we formalize this criterion as compositional generalization.

Notation.  We use uppercase letters for random variables and lowercase letters for their realizations. Let zt=(z1,t,…,zK,t)z_{t}=(z_{1,t},\ldots,z_{K,t}) denote true underlying state of the environment, where each component corresponds to a semantic factor of variation11 1 We include only factors that vary over the training distribution. For example, if a block remains gray throughout training, its color is not included in ztz_{t}. (Schölkopf et al., 2021), such as object position or end-effector pose. We model observations as st=f⁡(zt)s_{t}=f(z_{t}), where ff maps ztz_{t} to the RGB observation sts_{t} presented to the world model. An action-paired trajectory τ=(s0,a0,s1,a1,…,sH)\tau=(s_{0},a_{0},s_{1},a_{1},\ldots,s_{H}) can therefore equivalently be represented through the corresponding sequence of physical factors and actions, (z0,a0,z1,a1,…,zH),(z_{0},a_{0},z_{1},a_{1},\ldots,z_{H}), where HH denotes horizon.

3.1 Action-Conditioned Prediction Can Degenerate into Behavior Prediction

An action-conditioned world model should learn a transition predictor T^\hat{T} that receives sts_{t}22 2 For simplicity, sts_{t} may represent a finite history of states or observations. and an action ata_{t}, and predicts how the observation changes under the supplied action, T^​(st,at)≈st+1\hat{T}(s_{t},a_{t})\approx s_{t+1}. We consider the common offline setting in which data are collected by a behavior policy π\pi, so that the observed action satisfies at∼π(⋅∣st)a_{t}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid s_{t}). Thus, the observed transitions reflect the state–action pairings induced by π\pi, rather than arbitrary interventions at each state:

Tπ​(st+1∣st)=∫T⁡(st+1∣st,a)​π​(a∣st)​𝑑a.T^{\pi}(s_{t+1}\mid s_{t})=\int T(s_{t+1}\mid s_{t},a)\,\pi(a\mid s_{t})\,da. (1)

A predictor trained only on such data may degenerate into an action-ignorant model for state regions with restricted conditional action support, fitting the observed transitions by approximating

T^​(st+1∣st,at)≈Tπ​(st+1∣st),\hat{T}(s_{t+1}\mid s_{t},a_{t})\approx T^{\pi}(s_{t+1}\mid s_{t}), (2)

where the dependence on the supplied action ata_{t} is effectively lost.

3.2 Compositional Distribution Shifts in World Models

Now, let gtrg_{\mathrm{tr}} and gteg_{\mathrm{te}} denote the training and test goals. Each goal induces a behavior policy, πtr\pi_{\mathrm{tr}} or πte\pi_{\mathrm{te}}, which generates actions along the same environment dynamics TT. We denote the resulting trajectory distributions by ptrp_{\mathrm{tr}} and ptep_{\mathrm{te}}, respectively. We define the supports of physical factors and actions observed across trajectories, writing the training joint state–action support as

𝒞tr:=⋃t=0H−1suppptr⁡(Z1,t,…,ZK,t,At).\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{tr}}:=\bigcup_{t=0}^{H-1}\operatorname{supp}_{p_{\mathrm{tr}}}(Z_{1,t},\ldots,Z_{K,t},A_{t}). (3)

We also define the marginal support of each factor as 𝒵ktr:=⋃t=0H−1suppptr⁡(Zk,t)\mathcal{Z}_{k}^{\mathrm{tr}}:=\bigcup_{t=0}^{H-1}\operatorname{supp}_{p_{\mathrm{tr}}}(Z_{k,t}), and the action support as 𝒜tr:=⋃t=0H−1suppptr⁡(At)\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{tr}}:=\bigcup_{t=0}^{H-1}\operatorname{supp}_{p_{\mathrm{tr}}}(A_{t}). These supports pool over temporal position: a physical factor is considered observed during training if it occurs at any point along a trajectory drawn from ptrp_{\mathrm{tr}}. The test supports 𝒞te\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{te}}, 𝒵kte\mathcal{Z}_{k}^{\mathrm{te}}, and 𝒜te\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{te}} are defined analogously under ptep_{\mathrm{te}}. We define the combinatorial space as the Cartesian product of the marginal training supports:

𝒞×:=(∏k=1K𝒵ktr)×𝒜tr.\mathcal{C}^{\times}:=\left(\prod_{k=1}^{K}\mathcal{Z}_{k}^{\mathrm{tr}}\right)\times\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{tr}}. (4)

We study compositional distribution shifts (Liu et al., 2023; Mahajan et al., 2025) where the underlying transition dynamics are invariant across the train and test distribution, i.e., Ttr​(st+1∣st,at)=Tte​(st+1∣st,at)T_{{\mathrm{tr}}}(s_{t+1}\mid s_{t},a_{t})=T_{{\mathrm{te}}}(s_{t+1}\mid s_{t},a_{t}), but the test support introduces state, action pairs not present in the training support (𝒞te⊄𝒞tr\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{te}}\not\subset\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{tr}}). AnyGoal targets the combinatorial gap, regions of the combinatorial space 𝒞×\mathcal{C}^{\times} that are absent from the training joint support 𝒞tr\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{tr}}. Since test trajectories need not cover the entire gap or lie only within it, we require 𝒞te⊆𝒞×\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{te}}\subseteq\mathcal{C}^{\times} and choose goals with substantial mass in under-covered regions of 𝒞×\mathcal{C}^{\times}. This means that the test distribution does not introduce novel physical factors or actions, only novel combinations of observed physical factors and actions. Importantly, training-distribution accuracy does not identify the extension of the learned transition function to 𝒞×∖𝒞tr\mathcal{C}^{\times}\setminus\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{tr}}: predictors that agree on the training support may disagree on novel compositions (Wiedemer et al., 2024b). This motivates evaluating the combinatorial gap directly. We discuss more about why it is an essential test in Appendix A.

4 AnyGoal: Controlled Goal-Shift Evaluation

We introduce AnyGoal, a benchmark for testing whether world models generalize beyond the goal-directed trajectories on which they are trained. AnyGoal uses the controlled goal shifts discussed in Sec. 3.2 and builds on four widely used world-model tasks: TwoRoom (Sobal et al., 2025), Push-T (Chi et al., 2025), DMC Manipulator Insert-Peg (Tassa et al., 2018), and OGBench Cube (Park et al., 2025). AnyGoal contains eight variants: one free-space variant per base task and one or two contact-rich variants except TwoRoom. We release 400 episodes per variant, with data-collection tools for generating additional datasets. Figure 2 summarizes the tasks, with details in Appendix B.

4.1 AnyGoal Targets the Combinatorial Gap

Validating 𝒞𝐭𝐞⊆𝒞×\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{te}}\subseteq\mathcal{C}^{\times}.  For each base–target task pair, we apply three factor-wise support checks to verify that the target distribution remains marginally in-distribution relative to its reference distribution. The range check requires all query samples to lie within the coordinate-wise reference range. The Mahalanobis check uses the reference mean and covariance, thresholds distances at the reference 0.990.99-quantile, and requires at least 95%95\% of query samples to fall below it. The KDE check thresholds reference densities at the 0.010.01-quantile and requires at least 95%95\% of query samples to lie above it. The final support verdict is the conjunction of all three checks. All AnyGoal variants are designed to pass these factor-wise checks, which indicates that all tasks lie within the combinatorial space of training data. Appendix C provides the full details of pass-criterion definitions, the verified factor groups for each base task, and the complete score of range, Mahalanobis, and KDE results.

Measuring combinatorial-gap coverage of 𝒞𝐭𝐞\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{te}}.  We then estimate how much each target distribution overlaps with the base-task joint support. Unlike the factor-wise checks above, this joint test is meant to diagnose the combinatorial gap: individual factors may be marginally familiar while their full state–action combination is rare under the training distribution. For each base–target pair, we concatenate the action, agent state, and task-object or target state, fit a full-dimensional Gaussian KDE to the reference vectors, and set the density threshold to the empirical 0.010.01-quantile of log-densities. We then report the fraction of target vectors whose log-density exceeds this threshold. Lower joint scores indicate less overlap with the base-task joint distribution and greater coverage of the combinatorial gap. Full vector definitions and KDE implementation details are in Appendix D.

4.2 Relative Evaluation Against Base Tasks

We evaluate rollout prediction error and downstream MPC planning. Models are trained only on the base dataset and evaluated on both base and goal-shifted trajectories to measure relative changes. Rollout-error changes more directly diagnose whether action-conditioned dynamics generalize to unseen state–action combinations. However, planning success remains important. For JEPA-style models, it provides complementary evidence that the representation retains task-relevant information. For generative models, low rollout error can miss small but task-critical observation changes. We therefore report both metrics over seeds 0,1,20,1,2. Evaluation details are in Appendix H

Prediction Error. We measure MSE in each model’s native prediction space, which may be a learned latent space, oracle state space, or pixel space depending on the model class. We evaluate autoregressive prediction over horizons of 5 and 25 environment steps, with frame skip of 5. For each seed, we sample 100 episodes and average over all valid starting points within each episode.

MPC Planning Success Rate. We evaluate downstream control using the same CEM-based MPC implementation from Stable-WorldModel (Maes et al., 2026a) for all models. We use identical planning configurations, with a planning horizon of 25 environment steps. The full 25-step action sequence is executed before replanning.

4.3 AnyGoal Library and Evaluation Interface

We release AnyGoal as an open-source Python library for reproducible goal-shift evaluation. The library provides dataset access, task-specific data collection, and standardized rollout-prediction and MPC-planning evaluation across supported world models. Its unified CLI allows researchers to evaluate the same base-trained model on both the original task and unseen goals, with explicit model, dataset, and seed selection. The library also exposes Python APIs for dataset collection, model training, and evaluation. We provide examples and reproducibility instructions in Appendix K, with complete documentation available online.

5 Experiment and Results

We evaluate a diverse model suite spanning JEPA-style and generative objectives, learned and frozen visual encoders, and action-conditioning mechanisms (Tab. 1). To separate dynamics learning from visual representation failure, we also include oracle-state predictors which replace visual encoders with oracle states. For consistency, all models use frame skip 55 and one-step prediction. Model details and oracle-state variables for each environment are provided in Appendix F, and the full numerical results are summarized in Appendix I.1.

End-to-End World Models.  LeWorldModel (LeWM) (Maes et al., 2026b) is an end-to-end JEPA that jointly learns a visual encoder and an action-conditioned transformer predictor from pixels. It uses SIGReg (Balestriero and LeCun, 2025) for anti-collapse regularization and conditions the predictor through AdaLN (Peebles and Xie, 2023). Sensorimotor World Model (SMWM) (Ivashkov et al., 2026) uses the same encoder–predictor family as LeWM with an inverse-dynamics objective that encourages representations to retain controllable changes. DINO-WM (Zhou et al., 2025) decouples perception from dynamics by using a frozen DINOv2 (Oquab et al., 2024) patch encoder and predicting future patch representations, with actions concatenated to the patch tokens. DriftWorld (Lu et al., 2026) is a generative model that uses an action-conditioned spatial–temporal U-Net to predict future observations directly from observation history, actions, and noise. IRASim (Zhu et al., 2024) is a latent generative model that encodes observations with a frozen pretrained VAE and uses a Diffusion Transformer (Peebles and Xie, 2023) to predict future latents conditioned on action trajectories.

Oracle-State Predictor.  AdaLN predictor follows the architecture used by LeWM and SMWM. Action-Concatenated predictor follows the DINO-WM predictor, where an embedded action is concatenated to the patch representation before being processed by a causal transformer. Toy-DriftWorld is adapted from DriftWorld’s action-conditioned generative backbone. We use a reduced DriftWorld-style model and replace pixel inputs and outputs with true state inputs and next-state targets.

5.1 Dimensions of Goal-Shift Performance

Goal-shift performance cannot be summarized by a single number. The same degradation can reflect different sources depending on whether it appears in prediction or planning, in latent or pixel space, in free-space or contact-rich tasks, and with or without oracle state access. We therefore organize the results around five recurring dimensions for interpreting the results:

5.2 Dynamics Generalization Beyond Representation Failure

To examine dynamics generalization, we use the oracle states provided by AnyGoal, which expose task-relevant factors for action-conditioned next-step prediction and remove the need to infer them from observations under goal shifts. Overall, oracle-state predictors show that the AnyGoal gap cannot be reduced to visual representation failure.

Oracle-state predictors reveal an interaction-dependent dynamics gap.  Figure 6 shows that removing visual abstraction does not yield a uniform outcome across AnyGoal variants. In free-space variants such as TR-Route, Avoid-T, Avoid-Peg, and Cube-Hop, MPC performance is preserved or improves relative to the corresponding base task. In contrast, contact-rich variants consistently degrade, despite using the same privileged state inputs. This suggests that the difficulty is not merely access to the relevant state factors (Klindt et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2026), but whether the goal shift requires precise object interaction. This asymmetry is consistent with prior work showing that compositional generalization requires constraints on the learned function. Additive or interaction-free settings are especially favorable, since factor-specific mechanisms can be learned from observed compositions and reused under novel recombinations (Dong and Ma, 2022; Lachapelle et al., 2023; Wiedemer et al., 2024a; Mahajan et al., 2025). This intuition aligns with the independent causal mechanisms principle, under which reusable mechanisms remain autonomous as their joint occurrence changes (Parascandolo et al., 2018). Contact-rich variants depart from this favorable regime: action effects may no longer decompose into reusable factor-specific mechanisms. Compositional generalization may still be possible, but only with additional structure on these interactions (Brady et al., 2025). The same asymmetry appears in rollout prediction. Contact-rich variants show much larger error increases, often by one to three orders of magnitude, even with oracle states. Free-space variants degrade far less, and in some cases match or improve on the base-task error. Thus, removing representation learning does not make goal-shifted dynamics prediction uniformly reliable.

Metric alignment depends on task complexity.  We additionally observe that rollout error and planning performance sometimes diverge in free-space variants where planning can tolerate imperfect prediction. The closer agreement in contact-rich settings may reflect the structure of the planning problem. Rollout error measures whether the model predicts the full trajectory accurately, whereas MPC only needs to find some action sequence that reaches the goal, regardless of the exact intermediate path. Free-space tasks often admit many such trajectories, while contact-rich tasks allow fewer viable sequences because success also depends on the correct object interaction.

5.3 Representation Effects in End-to-End World Models

End-to-end world models can degrade on both metric under the goal shift even when oracle-state predictors remain stable. Such cases show that the AnyGoal gap is not solely a failure of action-conditioned dynamics, but can also reflect encoder failure under unseen factor combinations. Due to space constraints, we discuss two main observations, and more are in Appendix I.3.

Factor recombination can induce observation-level shifts.  AnyGoal controls generalization at the level of physical factors, but end-to-end models observe rendered inputs s=f⁡(z)s=f(z). Recombining marginally familiar factors can therefore create observations outside the joint visual support of expert rollouts, adding an encoder-inference challenge beyond dynamics prediction. (See Appendix I.2 for details.) Crucially, correct factor inference on training observations need not extend to unseen compositions. Even when factors are identifiable in distribution, an encoder may fail to invert novel recombined observations without compositional-consistency constraints (Wiedemer et al., 2024a). Thus, end-to-end world models face a representation-level generalization problem before dynamics prediction is considered. End-to-end models must therefore infer task-relevant factors from observations generated by unseen factor combinations, in addition to learning dynamics.

Latent geometry shapes degradation under goal shifts.

TwoRoom provides a useful case where end-to-end degradation cannot be attributed to an observation-level shift. Because agent position is the only changing factor and TR-Route positions remain marginally within the TwoRoom training support, the corresponding observations stay visually in support, enabling a controlled comparison between end-to-end models and oracle-state predictors. Figure 8 (a) summarizes results from TwoRoom and TR-Route across different model families. Even without an apparent visual shift, end-to-end models degrade whereas oracle-state predictors remain stable. This indicates that representation quality still matters: the learned latent space may fail to preserve the agent location precisely, introduce unnecessary dimensions or nuisance variation, or organize states in a geometry that is unfavorable for prediction and planning. Thus, even visually in-support goal shifts can fail if the learned latent geometry is not aligned with the task-relevant state geometry.

5.4 Diagnosing Behavior-Policy Shortcuts Through Action Sensitivity

As discussed in Sec. 3.1, a world model trained on expert rollouts may exploit correlations between states and the actions typically taken by the expert, rather than learning the effects of the supplied action. We investigate whether this failure mode is reflected in the learned models by measuring their sensitivity to interventional action inputs.

Interventional action sensitivity. To test whether the model responds to the supplied action rather than relying on the behavior policy’s preferred transition, we intervene on the action input while holding the state fixed. For each training state ss with observed action aa, we replace aa with actions from a fixed interventional set 𝒜cf\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{cf}} and measure the resulting change in the model’s predicted representation:

Sθ​(s)=1|𝒜cf|​∑a′∈𝒜cf‖ϕθ​(s,a)−ϕθ​(s,a′)‖2,S_{\theta}(s)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{cf}}|}\sum_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{cf}}}\left\|\phi_{\theta}(s,a)-\phi_{\theta}(s,a^{\prime})\right\|_{2}, (5)

where ϕθ​(s,a)\phi_{\theta}(s,a) denotes the model representation used for the sensitivity measurement. A smaller score indicates that the model is less sensitive to changes in the supplied action, although this does not necessarily imply incorrect predictions. We evaluate this score across training states and relate it to an environment-specific coordinate along which expert behavior is strongly biased. More details are in Appendix E.

Goal bias and reduced action sensitivity. Figure 9 shows that action sensitivity varies systematically with the state regions associated with expert behavior. In TwoRoom, expert trajectories favor motion toward the narrow passage. In Push-T, the agent typically approaches the block before pushing it. In Insert-Peg, the agent carries the grasped peg toward the target and in Cube, vertical actions are prevalent at low end-effector heights. Across these environments, we observe reduced sensitivity to interventional actions in regions where the training behavior is strongly constrained by the goal and these observations are consistent with the degeneracy described in Sec. 3.1.

6 Towards world models that generalize compositionally

Our oracle-state experiments show that compositional failures cannot be attributed only to visual representation learning. Even when task-relevant physical state is provided directly, goal shifts remain difficult, particularly when prediction involves contact-rich interactions. This raises a broader question for future work: what assumptions on the dynamics, data, and learned representation are sufficient for a world model to generalize compositionally? We see two distinct challenges.

A simple illustrative case. One favorable case for extrapolation in interaction-rich dynamics arises when, within each interaction regime, each transition mechanism depends only on a small subset of the state and action variables. Consider regime-dependent dynamics of the following form zt+1=Trt​(zt,at)z_{t+1}=T_{r_{t}}(z_{t},a_{t}), where rtr_{t} denotes an interaction regime, such as free motion, contact, or grasping. Both the autonomous state evolution and the effect of the action may therefore change across regimes. Suppose that, within a fixed regime rr, the transition of each next-state factor zk,t+1z_{k,t+1} depends only on a subset of the coordinates of (zt,at)(z_{t},a_{t}). Writing xt=(zt,at)x_{t}=(z_{t},a_{t}), this sparse dependence can be expressed as follows, ‖∇xTk,rt​(x)‖0≪dim(x)\left\|\nabla_{x}T_{k,r_{t}}(x)\right\|_{0}\ll\dim(x).

Let uku_{k} denote the relevant state and action coordinates for kk-th transition mechanism Tk,rtT_{k,r_{t}}, so that we may write zk,t+1=Tk,rt​(uk,t)z_{k,t+1}=T_{k,r_{t}}(u_{k,t}). This allows a simple case where compositional shift in the full state–action space need not require extrapolation for each transition mechanism.

𝒞te⊈𝒞tr,while𝒰kte⊆𝒰ktr∀k\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{te}}\not\subseteq\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{tr}},\qquad\text{while}\qquad\mathcal{U}_{k}^{\mathrm{te}}\subseteq\mathcal{U}_{k}^{\mathrm{tr}}\quad\forall\,k

where 𝒰ktr\mathcal{U}_{k}^{\mathrm{tr}} and 𝒰kte\mathcal{U}_{k}^{\mathrm{te}} denote the train and test supports of uku_{k} for the fixed regime rr. Thus, the complete state–action composition may be unseen, while every input relevant to predicting each next-state factor remains within its training support. Hence, if the corresponding mechanisms have been correctly learned, we can generalize to novel compositions as we do not need to extrapolate any individual mechanism beyond its training support. Appendix J (Proposition 1) gives a formal statement.

7 Conclusion

We introduced AnyGoal, a benchmark for evaluating whether world models generalize to new behavioral goals by recombining familiar states and actions. Across a diverse set of models, goal-shift generalization remains difficult even when the relevant state and action factors are marginally covered by the training distribution. Together, these analyses show that goal-shift failures are heterogeneous, reflecting interactions among representation, dynamics prediction, task structure, and evaluation metric. More broadly, AnyGoal connects world-model evaluation with compositional generalization. It asks for prediction on novel joint state–action combinations within the product of marginal training supports, a reasonable but unresolved requirement for reusable dynamics. Our theoretical perspective suggests that global coverage of all state–action combinations is neither realistic nor necessary. Instead, world models need coverage of local mechanism inputs, together with objectives or architectures that identify action-conditioned mechanisms rather than behavior-policy shortcuts. By isolating goal-induced recombination as a failure mode, AnyGoal provides a controlled basis for evaluating progress toward world models that learn reusable dynamics beyond expert rollouts.
