Appendix A Compositional Generalization: Essential World-Model Test

We formalize why our compositional evaluation is an essential test for world models. The key distinction is between extrapolating to unseen factors and recombining observed ones. Good action-conditioned world model should predict the effect of an observed action on familiar physical factors, even when that particular combination was not selected by the behavior policy.

For clarity, consider a deterministic oracle-state setting with true controlled dynamics zt+1=T⋆​(zt,at).z_{t+1}=T^{\star}(z_{t},a_{t}). Suppose the offline dataset is collected by a behavior policy a=πE​(z)a=\pi_{E}(z). Then the observed state–action support lies on the policy graph,

ΓπE={(z,a):a=πE​(z)}.\Gamma_{\pi_{E}}=\{(z,a):a=\pi_{E}(z)\}. (6)

Thus, expert rollouts cover only the state–action pairings induced by the behavior policy, not arbitrary interventions with observed actions.

Zero Training Error Does Not Imply Action-Conditioned Dynamics.

A predictive world model trained on (z,a,z′)∼ptr(z,a,z^{\prime})\sim p_{\mathrm{tr}} is constrained only on the state–action pairs generated by the behavior policy. Since observed actions satisfy a=πE​(z)a=\pi_{E}(z), the training loss constrains T^​(z,πE​(z))\hat{T}(z,\pi_{E}(z)), but not T^​(z,a)\hat{T}(z,a) for alternative observed actions at the same state. Consequently, the action-ignorant predictor

T^deg​(z,a)=T⋆​(z,πE​(z))\hat{T}_{\mathrm{deg}}(z,a)=T^{\star}(z,\pi_{E}(z)) (7)

achieves zero prediction error on the behavior dataset while ignoring the queried action aa. Thus, expert-rollout prediction cannot distinguish a controlled dynamics model from a predictor that only models behavior-policy transitions.

Compositional Evaluation Requires Action-Conditioned Dynamics

Compositional evaluation rules out this degenerate solution. Assume actions have nonzero effect within the observed marginal supports: for a set of oracle states with positive measure, there exist observed actions a,a′∈𝒜tra,a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{tr}} such that

T⋆​(z,a)≠T⋆​(z,a′).T^{\star}(z,a)\neq T^{\star}(z,a^{\prime}).

Now consider any action-ignorant predictor T^​(z,a)=h​(z)\hat{T}(z,a)=h(z). If it were correct on the relevant compositional state–action space, then for every observed action a∈𝒜tra\in\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{tr}}, h⁡(z)=T⋆​(z,a).h(z)=T^{\star}(z,a). Therefore, for any two observed actions a,a′a,a^{\prime},

T⋆​(z,a)=h⁡(z)=T⋆​(z,a′),T^{\star}(z,a)=h(z)=T^{\star}(z,a^{\prime}), (8)

which contradicts the action-relevance assumption. Hence, no action-ignorant model can be correct on recombinations of observed state and action factors when actions causally affect the next state.

Appendix B AnyGoal Task Details

B.1 Two Room and Its Variants

TwoRoom is a simple navigation environment with two rooms connected by a narrow slot. The agent must move through the slot and reach a target location, with little to no meaningful interaction with the environment beyond collision with walls. Because the dynamics are essentially planar motion, this environment isolates whether models can preserve action-conditioned movement under goal-biased trajectory data.

TwoRoom Route is an interaction-light navigation variant. The agent must follow a piecewise-linear triangular route defined by a start point, an intermediate waypoint, and an invisible endpoint, rather than moving directly through the slot toward the target. Episodes mix clean, noisy, and variable-speed actions within the observed action support. This variant tests whether the model preserves planar action-conditioned dynamics when familiar positions and actions are recombined outside the dominant slot-crossing behavior of the base dataset.

B.2 PushT and Its Variants

PushT is a planar manipulation environment where the agent must push a T-shaped block into a fixed T-shaped goal pose. Unlike TwoRoom, the base task already requires meaningful contact, object translation, and object rotation. The expert trajectories are strongly goal-directed, coupling agent motion with the block pose and the target configuration. This environment tests whether world models learn action-conditioned contact dynamics rather than only the dominant expert pushing manifold.

AvoidT is a non-interactive variant. The agent must avoid touching the physical T-block and move to one of four corner regions. This variant keeps the agent and action factors familiar, but changes the required behavior from goal-directed pushing to free-space navigation around the object. It primarily tests whether the model preserves the action effect when the expert pushing objective is no longer appropriate.

StackT is an interaction-rich variant. The physical T-block must be placed so that its head overlaps with the fixed goal T, while its rotation is opposite to the original PushT goal orientation, creating a plus-shaped target configuration. This variant requires contact and rotation dynamics under a goal that differs from the original training objective.

PushT Anti-goal is also interaction-rich and directly reverses the dominant goal bias in the base dataset. The physical T-block is initialized near the original PushT goal pose, but the agent must push it away from the fixed goal region and move it toward one of four corner regions, with rotation opposite to the original goal orientation. This tests whether the model can predict familiar pushing dynamics when the required behavior contradicts the original expert trajectory distribution.

B.3 Insert-Peg and Its Variants

Insert-Peg is a planar manipulation environment where an arm must move a peg toward a sampled slot and insert it into the target opening. The task involves articulated robot motion, object contact, and alignment between the peg and the slot. Expert trajectories are strongly structured around successful insertion behavior. This environment tests whether models can learn action-conditioned manipulation dynamics under goal-biased contact-rich data.

Avoid-Peg is an interaction-light variant. The arm must move around the target box in a specified hugging direction while avoiding contact with the peg. This changes the goal-conditioned arm behavior without requiring peg manipulation, testing whether the model can predict familiar arm motion under a non-insertion objective.

Extract-Peg is an interaction-rich variant. The arm must extract the peg from the target box, move it through a waypoint, and place it at a destination, with episodes balanced between left- and right-side box placements. This reverses the dominant insertion behavior while keeping the peg, box, workspace, and action space familiar.

B.4 OGBench Cube and Its Variants

Cube is a robot manipulation environment where the end-effector must interact with a cube and move it toward a target configuration. The base behavior follows a structured pick-and-place pattern, including approach, grasp, lift, transport, and release. This creates a goal-biased trajectory distribution in which robot motion, gripper state, cube pose, and target location are tightly coupled. The environment tests whether models learn manipulation dynamics beyond this dominant expert sequence.

CubeHop is a non-interactive variant. The robot does not intentionally move the cube. Instead, the end-effector moves between waypoint and target positions while gradually changing its yaw. This variant changes the goal-conditioned end-effector behavior while avoiding object interaction. It tests whether the model can predict familiar robot motion and yaw changes outside the dominant cube-manipulation trajectory distribution.

CubeDiagonal is an interaction-rich variant. The robot manipulates the cube using a diagonal grasp configuration, where the gripper contacts opposite edges of the cube instead of the standard parallel faces. This introduces a novel contact regime with different grasp geometry while keeping the object, task objective, and action space unchanged. It tests whether the model can compose familiar manipulation factors under unseen interaction configurations.

Appendix C Statistical Test 1: Marginal Distribution Support

C.1 Distribution Support Criteria

We describe the statistical criteria used to decide whether a query distribution remains inside the support of a reference distribution. Let P={pn}n=1NP=\{p_{n}\}_{n=1}^{N} denote the reference or training point set, and let Q={qm}m=1MQ=\{q_{m}\}_{m=1}^{M} denote the query point set.

For each factor, we compute the empirical mean μP=1N​∑n=1Npn\mu_{P}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}p_{n} and regularized covariance ΣP=Cov⁡(P)+λ​I\Sigma_{P}=\operatorname{Cov}(P)+\lambda I, where λ>0\lambda>0 is a small diagonal regularizer used to ensure that the covariance matrix is invertible. This is particularly important for low-rank or manifold-valued factors, such as circular variables represented by sine and cosine coordinates.

Now we measure three metric respectively. First, the Mahalanobis criterion checks whether query points remain within the reference distribution’s main covariance structure.

Second, the KDE criterion checks whether query points lie in regions with sufficient empirical reference density, beyond an ellipsoidal approximation.

Lastly, the range criterion checks whether query points avoid direct coordinate-wise extrapolation beyond the observed marginal range.

The final verdict is the conjunction of all non-ignored criteria:

pass⁡(Q;P)=range⁡(Q;P)∧Mahalanobis0.99⁡(Q;P)∧KDE0.01⁡(Q;P).\operatorname{pass}(Q;P)=\operatorname{range}(Q;P)\wedge\operatorname{Mahalanobis}_{0.99}(Q;P)\wedge\operatorname{KDE}_{0.01}(Q;P). (13)

If the observed-range criterion is ignored for a circular factor, the verdict is computed over the remaining criteria:

pass⁡(Q;P)=Mahalanobis0.99⁡(Q;P)∧KDE0.01⁡(Q;P).\operatorname{pass}(Q;P)=\operatorname{Mahalanobis}_{0.99}(Q;P)\wedge\operatorname{KDE}_{0.01}(Q;P). (14)

This design separates marginal factor support from full trajectory-distribution typicality. The support checks are applied at the level of semantic factor groups to verify that each physical factor remains within the reference support. Combinatorial novelty can still arise when individually supported factors appear in new joint configurations that are rare or absent under the expert trajectory distribution.

C.2 Verified Factor Groups

We apply the three support criteria above to task-relevant factor groups rather than to the full joint state–action vector. This verifies marginal coverage of the physical factors and actions used in each goal-shifted variant, while allowing the full combinations to remain novel. Table 2 lists the factor groups checked for each reference–query pair.

C.3 Support-Verification Results

Table 3 reports the full support-verification results for the factor groups in Table 2. For each reference–query pair, we report the pass rate under the Mahalanobis, KDE, and observed-range criteria, together with the final conjunction verdict. All checked factors pass, confirming that the AnyGoal variants remain marginally in distribution with respect to the corresponding base datasets.

Appendix D Statistical Test 2: Full-Dimensional Joint Distribution Support

We complement the factor-wise support tests in Table 3 with a full-dimensional joint test. The factor-wise tests verify whether each task-relevant factor or factor group is marginally supported by the reference data. In contrast, the joint test asks whether the complete state–action combination lies in a high-density region of the reference distribution. This test uses the concatenated vectors directly, without coordinate marginalization or worst-pair reduction.

For each transition, let aa denote the action, sagents_{\mathrm{agent}} the agent-observed state, and sothers_{\mathrm{other}} the task-object and target state. We evaluate three joint vectors:

zagent=sagent,zall=[sagent,sother],za,all=[a,sagent,sother].z_{\mathrm{agent}}=s_{\mathrm{agent}},\qquad z_{\mathrm{all}}=[s_{\mathrm{agent}},s_{\mathrm{other}}],\qquad z_{a,\mathrm{all}}=[a,s_{\mathrm{agent}},s_{\mathrm{other}}].

Only rows that are finite in every coordinate of the corresponding vector are retained. Thus, terminal rows with undefined actions contribute to the state-only vectors but not to the action–state vector.

For each reference vector set, we quantize each coordinate using reference-based limits with small padding, and assign zero density to target values outside these limits. We then whiten the quantized vectors using the full reference covariance with a small diagonal regularizer. This preserves correlations between action and state coordinates when computing kernel distances.

We fit a full-dimensional Gaussian KDE to the whitened reference vectors using Scott’s bandwidth rule. The density is evaluated without reference subsampling, dimension dropping, nearest-neighbor truncation, or pairwise marginalization. The density threshold is calibrated only from the reference samples:

τ=Q0.01​({log⁡p^​(xi)}i=1N).\tau=Q_{0.01}\!\left(\{\log\widehat{p}(x_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}\right). (15)

For target vectors Y={yj}j=1MY=\{y_{j}\}_{j=1}^{M}, we report the fraction whose log-density exceeds this reference-sample threshold:

ID(Y;X)=1M∑j=1M[logp^(yj)≥τ].\operatorname{ID}(Y;X)=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\mathbf{1}\!\left[\log\widehat{p}(y_{j})\geq\tau\right]. (16)

The joint score is therefore a full-vector KDE support percentage. Individual factors can pass their marginal support tests while the concatenated vector has a low joint score, indicating that the corresponding combination of familiar values is rare under the reference distribution.

Appendix E Interventional Action Set

For each environment, we choose a fixed interventional action set that remains within the empirical action support while covering the task-relevant intervention directions as uniformly as possible. For environments with direct 2D controls, this is a regular grid in action space. For higher-dimensional manipulation actions, we vary only the dimensions needed for the intended spatial intervention and keep the remaining dimensions fixed.

TwoRoom.

For TwoRoom, actions are two-dimensional position deltas, so interventional interventions are defined directly in the action space. We use a fixed 3×33\times 3 grid that is uniformly spread over the two action dimensions and includes the zero action as the center intervention.

Push-T.

For Push-T, actions are also two-dimensional planar controls. We therefore use a fixed 3×33\times 3 grid in the planar action space. The grid is chosen to provide evenly distributed in-distribution interventions at the empirical action scale of the dataset.

Insert-Peg.

Unlike the 2D navigation and planar pushing tasks, Insert-Peg actions are 5-dimensional motor commands rather than direct task-space displacements. Therefore, interventional actions cannot be chosen by simply placing actions on a Euclidean grid in task space. Instead, we select actions by their realized effect on the hand endpoint.

We first choose a representative state near the center of the expert-state distribution. Each candidate action is sampled from the dataset and repeated for five environment control steps from this same state. We then measure the resulting hand endpoint in the xx-zz plane. To ensure that interventions remain in distribution, we retain only actions whose 20-nearest-neighbor distance in the raw 5D action space is below the 95th-percentile threshold estimated from held-out dataset actions.

Among the retained actions, we select a fixed set of nine interventional actions whose realized endpoints form the widest approximately uniform 3×33\times 3 grid. The zero action is assigned to the center, and the remaining actions are chosen to maximize grid spacing while keeping each endpoint within 10%10\% of its corresponding ideal grid point. The resulting grid spacing is 0.03580.0358, with a maximum endpoint mismatch of 9.95%9.95\% of the grid spacing.

Cube.

For Cube, the raw action is five-dimensional, but the interventional protocols are designed to probe spatial sensitivity of end-effector motion. We therefore vary only translational action dimensions and keep Δ​yaw\Delta\mathrm{yaw} and Δ​gripper\Delta\mathrm{gripper} fixed at zero. The horizontal protocol uses an xx-yy grid.

Implementation Detail.

Within orignal LeWM architecture, we measure action sensitivity using hidden representations from the predictor blocks. Let flf_{l} denote the last-token hidden representation after the ll-th ConditionalBlock,

fl=output[:, -1, :]f_{l}=\texttt{output[:, -1, :]}

obtained from a forward hook on model.predictor.transformer.layers[layer_idx]. Thus, flf_{l} is not the representation immediately after AdaLN modulation; it is the output of the full AdaLN-conditioned transformer block, including the attention and MLP residual updates. In all reported layer-wise analyses, we average the sensitivity scores across these block outputs. For the final prediction representation, we use pred[:, -1, :], the output of model.predict(...) after the final pred_proj layer.

Appendix F Model Explanation

Our model selection is designed to span several substantially different approaches to visual world modeling rather than to concentrate on a single architectural family. In particular, we evaluate both joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) and generative visual world models. Within the JEPA family, we include methods that jointly learn perception and dynamics from the offline dataset as well as a method that keeps a large pretrained visual encoder frozen. Within the generative family, we include both a direct action-conditioned generator and a latent video diffusion model with an explicit visual encoder–decoder. This diversity is important for our central question: whether goal-induced combinatorial bias is specific to a particular representation or generative objective, or can arise more broadly when action-conditioned prediction is trained on a biased offline distribution. For consistency, all models use frame skip 55, history length 33, and one-step prediction, except Sensorimotor-WM, where we keep the original history length 11 to preserve its inverse-dynamics setup.

F.1 End-to-End World Models

LeWorldModel (LeWM).

LeWorldModel (Maes et al., 2026b) is an end-to-end joint-embedding predictive architecture trained directly from pixels and actions. An image encoder maps observations to compact latent representations, and an autoregressive transformer predictor models the next latent representation conditioned on the action. Actions are injected into each transformer layer through adaptive layer normalization (AdaLN-zero). Unlike approaches that rely on a frozen encoder, stop-gradient target network, or exponential-moving-average encoder, LeWM jointly optimizes its encoder and predictor.

A central design choice in LeWM is its anti-collapse regularization. In addition to the next-embedding mean-squared prediction loss, LeWM applies the Sketched-Isotropic-Gaussian Regularizer (SIGReg), which encourages the empirical latent distribution to match an isotropic Gaussian. The resulting model is particularly useful for our study because it represents a recent example of a fully end-to-end JEPA in which both the visual representation and dynamics predictor are shaped by the same offline trajectories.

Sensorimotor World Model (SMWM).

The Sensorimotor World Model (Ivashkov et al., 2026) is also an end-to-end JEPA, but uses a different principle to prevent representation collapse. Rather than prescribing the marginal geometry of the latent representation, SMWM introduces an inverse dynamics model that predicts the executed action from consecutive latent states. The encoder, forward dynamics model, and inverse model are optimized jointly using forward-prediction and inverse-dynamics losses.

The inverse objective requires consecutive representations to preserve information that is useful for recovering the action that produced the transition. Consequently, the learned representation is explicitly biased toward controllable, action-relevant structure. Architecturally, SMWM adopts the LeWM encoder and transformer forward predictor, including AdaLN-zero action conditioning, while replacing Gaussian latent regularization with inverse dynamics as its anti-collapse mechanism. This makes SMWM particularly relevant to our benchmark: it provides a strong test of whether explicitly encouraging action-aware representations is sufficient to prevent failures induced by goal-biased state–action coverage.

DINO World Model (DINO-WM).

DINO-WM (Zhou et al., 2025) separates representation learning from dynamics learning. Instead of jointly learning an image encoder from the offline control dataset, it uses pretrained DINOv2 patch features as the observation representation and keeps the DINOv2 encoder frozen during both world-model training and evaluation. A causal ViT-based transition model then predicts future patch representations from a history of latent observations and actions.

DINO-WM also differs in how actions enter the predictor. The action is first mapped through an MLP and the resulting action representation is concatenated to each spatial patch representation before the transformer processes the latent state. Thus, compared with LeWM and SMWM, DINO-WM provides a useful separation between perception and dynamics: the visual representation is inherited from large-scale pretraining, while only the action-conditioned transition model is learned from the potentially goal-biased offline trajectories. This lets us test whether combinatorial failures persist even when the visual encoder itself is not learned from the biased task dataset.

DriftWorld.

DriftWorld (Lu et al., 2026) represents a substantially different, reconstruction-based family of world models. It is an action-conditioned generative model based on drifting rather than a JEPA or iterative diffusion model. Its core generator is a spatial–temporal U-Net that receives observation history, Gaussian noise, and a future action sequence and generates the corresponding future visual observations. Actions condition the U-Net frame-by-frame through FiLM, such that each future frame is explicitly conditioned on its corresponding action.

For relatively simple simulated domains such as PushT, DriftWorld operates directly in pixel space and does not require a learned visual state encoder between the observations and the action-conditioned generator. Its drifting objective moves generated samples toward ground-truth future observations and away from generated negatives, enabling future video generation in a single forward pass at inference time. DriftWorld therefore provides an important contrast to the latent JEPA models: prediction and visual generation are implemented by a single action-conditioned generative backbone rather than an explicit encoder followed by a latent dynamics predictor.

IRASim.

IRASim (Zhu et al., 2024) represents the latent generative end of our model suite. It formulates world modeling for robot manipulation as trajectory-conditioned video generation. Frames are first compressed using a pretrained VAE, after which a Diffusion Transformer (DiT) models future video latents conditioned on historical observations and a robot action trajectory. The generated latents are subsequently decoded back to RGB observations.

A defining component of IRASim is its fine-grained action conditioning. Rather than conditioning the complete video only on a global trajectory embedding, IRASim can associate individual actions with their corresponding generated frames through frame-level adaptive normalization. This architecture gives us a generative model that is structurally different from DriftWorld: visual prediction occurs in an encoded latent space, the dynamics generator is a diffusion transformer, and an explicit encoder–decoder surrounds the dynamics model.

F.2 Predictor-Only Models from True States

End-to-end evaluation mixes perception and dynamics-prediction errors. To isolate the latter, we use predictor-only models that replace the visual encoder with oracle states from simulator metadata and proprioceptive signals. These oracle states contain task-relevant physical variables, such as positions, orientations, agent or gripper configurations, and other environment-specific state factors needed for one-step prediction.

We refer to these inputs as oracle state representations rather than unique or minimal Markov states. Their role is operational: they provide the predictor with relevant physical information directly, removing visual representation learning as the explanation for prediction failure. We instantiate three predictor families derived from the end-to-end models above. The two transformer-based predictor-only models are trained with next-state mean-squared error,

ℒpred=‖s^t+1−st+1‖22.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pred}}=\left\|\hat{s}_{t+1}-s_{t+1}\right\|_{2}^{2}. (17)

Toy-DriftWorld instead retains the drifting particle loss used by its generative backbone.

AdaLN Transformer Predictor.

Our first predictor follows the forward-model architecture shared by LeWM and SMWM. Ground-truth state factors replace the learned visual embedding, while the action is injected into the transformer through AdaLN-zero. The transformer predicts the next true state directly. Because LeWM and SMWM use the same forward-predictor family, a single predictor-only architecture represents both models in this controlled setting. Their end-to-end distinction—SIGReg versus inverse-dynamics representation regularization—is intentionally removed once the encoder is replaced by the oracle state.

Action-Duplicated Transformer Predictor.

Our second predictor follows DINO-WM’s transition-model conditioning strategy. The true state replaces DINO patch features, while an embedded action is attached to the state representation before processing by a causal transformer. This preserves the central architectural distinction of DINO-WM’s predictor: action information enters through the predictor input rather than modulating transformer layers through AdaLN. The model is again trained only to regress the next true state with MSE.

DriftWorld-Style Generative Predictor.

Our third predictor is derived from the action-conditioned generative backbone of DriftWorld. Because DriftWorld does not require a separate visual encoder for the simple simulated setting, its U-Net constitutes the principal predictive computation. For the predictor-only experiment, we use a reduced-size version of this backbone and replace pixel observations and outputs with the corresponding true-state representation. The predictor retains the drifting particle loss while operating on oracle-state inputs and next-state targets.

F.2.1 Oracle States

Oracle-state predictors replace RGB observations with task-relevant physical state variables from each base environment.

F.2.2 Model Architecture Details

For LeWM (Maes et al., 2026b) and Sensorimotor World-Model (Ivashkov et al., 2026), we use the authors’ official implementations. For DINO-WM (Zhou et al., 2025), we use the Stable-WorldModel (Maes et al., 2026a) implementation without proprioceptive inputs. For DriftWorld (Lu et al., 2026), we use the authors’ implementation with two minor modifications: we integrate frame skip into the action-conditioning interface and add a pixel-space cost function for MPC planning, without changing the main architecture. We use the Push-T model configuration for TwoRoom and Push-T, and the Robomimic model configuration for the Cube and Manipulator environments. For IRASim (Zhu et al., 2024), we use the authors’ implementation with the same frame-skip integration and pixel-space planning cost, and use IRASim-XL/2 for all environments.

For the oracle-state experiments, we use three toy predictor families derived from the corresponding end-to-end modeling motifs. Toy-AdaLN keeps the LeWM transformer size unchanged, replacing only the pixel-latent input and output with true-state projections. Toy Action-Duplicate preserves the DINO-WM-style action duplication, causal masking, and shifted prediction design, but adapts it to scalar true-state tokens with a smaller 192D predictor instead of the original high-dimensional patch-token predictor. Toy-DriftWorld preserves the stochastic particle-generation objective and drifting loss, but replaces the image U-Net with a compact vector-valued residual FiLM MLP operating on oracle states.

Appendix G Training Details

AdaLN predictors and Action duplicated predictors use AdamW, batch size 256256, weight decay 10−310^{-3}, linear warmup followed by cosine decay, gradient clipping at 1.01.0, and an MSE loss over all shifted state predictions. Toy-DriftWorld is trained with AdamW, batch size 128128, learning rate 10−410^{-4}, weight decay 10−210^{-2}, a 500500-step warmup followed by a constant schedule, gradient clipping at 2.02.0, and the drifting particle loss. For end-to-end world models, we follow the original settings.

Appendix H Detailed Planning and Evaluation Configuration

All planning experiments use the same MPC evaluation pipeline based on the Stable World Model library Maes et al. (2026a), with Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) solver.

H.1 Planning Evaluation Criteria

Table 8 summarizes the success criteria used for each environment. Some details are below.

TwoRoom.

For TwoRoom, the goal is the dataset future agent position. A rollout is successful when ‖pt−pg‖2<16\|p_{t}-p_{g}\|_{2}<16, where ptp_{t} is the current agent position and pgp_{g} is the goal agent position. Distances are measured in pixels in the 224×224224\times 224 environment coordinate system. Target and door positions are not used.

PushT.

For PushT, the position error is computed over the 4D vector [agentx,agenty,blockx,blocky][\text{agent}_{x},\text{agent}_{y},\text{block}_{x},\text{block}_{y}]. A rollout is successful when both ‖stpos−sgpos‖2<20\|s_{t}^{\mathrm{pos}}-s_{g}^{\mathrm{pos}}\|_{2}<20 and dangle​(θt,θg)<π/9d_{\mathrm{angle}}(\theta_{t},\theta_{g})<\pi/9 hold at the same timestep. The angle distance accounts for object symmetries: square and + shapes use 90∘90^{\circ} symmetry, Z and I shapes use 180∘180^{\circ} symmetry, and other shapes use 360∘360^{\circ}.

Cube.

For Cube, the goal is defined by the dataset future end-effector pose and cube position. A rollout is successful when ‖pte​e−pge​e‖2≤0.04​m\|p_{t}^{ee}-p_{g}^{ee}\|_{2}\leq 0.04\,\mathrm{m}, |wrap⁡(ψge​e−ψte​e)|≤0.10​rad|\operatorname{wrap}(\psi_{g}^{ee}-\psi_{t}^{ee})|\leq 0.10\,\mathrm{rad}, and ‖ptc​u​b​e−pgc​u​b​e‖2≤0.04​m\|p_{t}^{cube}-p_{g}^{cube}\|_{2}\leq 0.04\,\mathrm{m} all hold at the same timestep. Cube orientation, gripper opening, contact, and velocity are not used. Once satisfied, episode-level success remains true. Cube rollouts are not terminated early by this criterion.

Manipulator Insert Peg.

For Manipulator Insert Peg, the goal is defined by the dataset future hand and peg poses. Positions are measured in the (x,z)(x,z) plane, and planar angles are computed from quaternion components (qw,qy)(q_{w},q_{y}) as 2​atan2⁡(qy,qw)2\operatorname{atan2}(q_{y},q_{w}). A rollout is successful when the hand position, hand angle, peg position, and peg angle errors are all within their thresholds: 0.04​m0.04\,\mathrm{m} for positions and 0.10​rad0.10\,\mathrm{rad} for angles. Arm joints, touch sensors, velocity, and the physical target or slot pose are not used. This dataset-goal success metric differs from the native task success based on the DeepMind Control shaped reward.

H.2 Configuration

We evaluated all true-state dynamics models using the same goal-conditioned receding-horizon controller. For each episode, the initial state and goal were sampled from the same dataset trajectory with a temporal offset of 25 environment steps. Planning was performed in the normalized action space using the cross-entropy method (CEM). Each candidate consisted of five action blocks, where each block contained five consecutive environment actions, yielding an effective planning horizon of 25 environment steps. At every planning round, CEM evaluated 300 candidate sequences for 30 iterations and refitted a factorized Gaussian distribution to the 30 lowest-cost elites. The objective was the squared Euclidean distance between the terminal predicted state and the goal in the model’s normalized state space. The final mean sequence was executed open-loop for all five action blocks before replanning. Episodes were evaluated for at most 50 environment steps, corresponding to at most two planning rounds.

Appendix I Results

I.1 Full Results

This section reports the full numerical results used in the main analysis. We include absolute MPC planning success rates complementing the relative comparisons shown in the main text, as well as table of relative prediction errors with absolute base-environment rollout errors. For the five-step prediction error, corresponding to 2525 environment steps, Avoid-T is omitted because its episodes are too short to support this horizon.

I.2 Factor Support versus Observation Support

Our compositional shifts are defined at the level of physical factors: test queries recombine factor values that are individually observed in the training data. However, this does not imply that the resulting observations are in-distribution for an end-to-end encoder.

Let 𝒵tr\mathcal{Z}^{\mathrm{tr}} denote the joint support of physical factors under the training trajectories, and let 𝒵×=∏k=1K𝒵ktr\mathcal{Z}^{\times}=\prod_{k=1}^{K}\mathcal{Z}^{\mathrm{tr}}_{k} denote the Cartesian product of their marginal supports. A compositional query may satisfy 𝒵te⊆𝒵×\mathcal{Z}^{\mathrm{te}}\subseteq\mathcal{Z}^{\times} while still containing factor combinations absent from 𝒵tr\mathcal{Z}^{\mathrm{tr}}.

End-to-end world models observe s=f⁡(z)s=f(z), where ff is the rendering map. Thus the corresponding observation supports are 𝒮tr=f⁡(𝒵tr)\mathcal{S}^{\mathrm{tr}}=f(\mathcal{Z}^{\mathrm{tr}}) and 𝒮×=f⁡(𝒵×)\mathcal{S}^{\times}=f(\mathcal{Z}^{\times}). When ff mixes factors, unseen factor combinations in 𝒵×∖𝒵tr\mathcal{Z}^{\times}\setminus\mathcal{Z}^{\mathrm{tr}} can induce observations in 𝒮×∖𝒮tr\mathcal{S}^{\times}\setminus\mathcal{S}^{\mathrm{tr}}.

Therefore, a query can be factor-wise in support while still creating an observation-level shift for an end-to-end encoder. This is why we separately analyze oracle-state predictors: they remove the encoder-inference problem and isolate whether the learned dynamics model can generalize across recombined state-action factors.

I.3 Additional Observations

Prediction Space Affects Metric Interpretation

We do not use the rollout results to directly rank JEPA-style and generative world models. These models predict in different spaces: JEPA-style models are evaluated in latent space, whereas generative models are evaluated in pixel or reconstruction space. As a result, absolute prediction errors are not directly comparable across model families, and we primarily interpret rollout degradation relative to each model’s own base-task performance.

Under this relative comparison, generative models often show smaller rollout degradation under some goal shifts, while several JEPA-style models show larger increases. However, this tendency does not translate consistently to planning: a model can show stable rollout error but poor MPC success, or larger rollout degradation while remaining competitive in control. We therefore treat prediction-space effects as an interpretation caveat rather than a model-family ranking. The results suggest that rollout robustness and downstream control utility are related but distinct properties.

Oracle state access does not guarantee better planning.

Interestingly, access to the oracle state does not always lead to stronger planning performance. In Cube, several end-to-end models achieve higher planning success than their oracle-state counterparts, both on the base task and on CubeDiagonal. This should not be interpreted as evidence that learned latents are generally superior to physical state representations, since the end-to-end and oracle predictors differ in more than just their input space.

Rather, these results suggest that state observability and planning suitability are distinct properties. Oracle states preserve the underlying physical factors, but the resulting geometry may not be the most favorable one for the planner’s cost and optimization procedure. Conversely, a learned representation may, in some cases, emphasize task-relevant variation or compress nuisance factors in a way that makes goal-directed optimization easier. We therefore treat planning performance as depending not only on how much state information is available, but also on how that information is organized in the representation space.

Appendix J Toward Compositional Generalization in World Models

Our experiments empirically show that removing visual abstraction is not sufficient for reliable goal-shift generalization: free-space dynamics often transfer across new state–action compositions, whereas contact-rich dynamics remain substantially harder even when the predictor receives task-relevant physical state directly. This raises a dynamics-level question: what structure must a world model learn for its dynamics to remain reusable under compositional shifts?

Ideally, we want to solve AnyGoal by learning reusable dynamics that extrapolate to the combinatorial space. That is, we want a learned transition function T^\hat{T} that matches the observed training transitions on 𝒞tr\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{tr}}, while also predicting correctly on novel compositions in 𝒞×∖𝒞tr\mathcal{C}^{\times}\setminus\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{tr}}. We separate this question into two parts: identifying reusable mechanisms on the training support, and extrapolating those mechanisms to novel compositions.

J.1 Identifying Reusable Mechanisms on the Training Support

To discuss identifiability, we first need to specify what structure the true transition may have. One observation from our results is that world models often face multiple regimes, such as free motion, contact, grasping, or collision.

In a single-regime setting with little interaction, such as free-space navigation of an agent, one may expect a transition of the form zt+1=f⁡(zt)+g⁡(at)z_{t+1}=f(z_{t})+g(a_{t}). In this favorable case, identifiability and compositional generalization are easier to obtain, for example through an additive function class (Dong and Ma, 2022; Lachapelle et al., 2023; Wiedemer et al., 2024b; Wiedemer et al., 2024a; Mahajan et al., 2025).

However, world-model dynamics are often regime-dependent and more complex than a purely additive and separated form. The action effect is usually better written as gr​(zt,at)g_{r}(z_{t},a_{t}) rather than g⁡(at)g(a_{t}), meaning that the transition cannot be decomposed into simple independent state-only and action-only terms. A simple additive form is therefore too limited for the setting we want to characterize.

We instead consider a factorized transition with regime-dependent local mechanisms. For each factor kk, let

zk,t+1=Tk,rt​(uk,t),uk,t=(zpa⁡(k),t,apa⁡(k),t),z_{k,t+1}=T_{k,r_{t}}(u_{k,t}),\qquad u_{k,t}=\bigl(z_{\mathrm{pa}(k),t},a_{\mathrm{pa}(k),t}\bigr),

where pa⁡(k)\mathrm{pa}(k) denotes the local parents of factor kk, and rt∈{1,…,R}r_{t}\in\{1,\ldots,R\} denotes a discrete local regime. The transition kernel is specified as follows

Trt​(zt,at)=(T1,rt​(u1,t),…,TK,rt​(uK,t)).T_{r_{t}}(z_{t},a_{t})=\bigl(T_{1,r_{t}}(u_{1,t}),\ldots,T_{K,r_{t}}(u_{K,t})\bigr).

Since multiple regime–mechanism decompositions can explain the same training transitions, we next state the favorable assumptions under which the discussion applies: a Markov, goal-invariant oracle state, and training-support identification of the relevant local mechanisms up to observational equivalence.

Assumption 1 (Markov and invariant oracle state)

The oracle state ztz_{t} is Markov, and the transition law is invariant across training and test goals:

p⁡(zt+1∣z≤t,a≤t)=p⁡(zt+1∣zt,at),Ttr​(zt+1∣zt,at)=Tte​(zt+1∣zt,at).p(z_{t+1}\mid z_{\leq t},a_{\leq t})=p(z_{t+1}\mid z_{t},a_{t}),\qquad T_{\mathrm{tr}}(z_{t+1}\mid z_{t},a_{t})=T_{\mathrm{te}}(z_{t+1}\mid z_{t},a_{t}).

Thus, goal shifts change the behavior distribution, but not the environment dynamics.

Assumption 2 (Identification of local mechanisms)

For each state factor kk, suppose that the interaction regime rtr_{t} and the local input uk,t=uk​(zt,at)u_{k,t}=u_{k}(z_{t},a_{t}) are observed or identifiable from the training transitions, and that the corresponding regime can be consistently inferred at prediction time.

zk,t+1=Tk,rt​(uk,t),z^k,t+1=T^k,rt​(uk,t).z_{k,t+1}=T_{k,r_{t}}(u_{k,t}),\qquad\hat{z}_{k,t+1}=\hat{T}_{k,r_{t}}(u_{k,t}).

For each factor and regime, define the training support

𝒰k,rtr:=⋃t=0H−1suppptr⁡(Uk,t∣Rt=r).\mathcal{U}^{\mathrm{tr}}_{k,r}:=\bigcup_{t=0}^{H-1}\operatorname{supp}_{p_{\mathrm{tr}}}(U_{k,t}\mid R_{t}=r).

Let ℒtr​(T~)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{tr}}(\tilde{T}) denote the population objective used to train the world model. We assume that this objective identifies the regime-conditioned mechanisms on their training support: any population minimizer T~\tilde{T} satisfies

T~k,r​(u)=Tk,r​(u),∀u∈𝒰k,rtr,\tilde{T}_{k,r}(u)=T_{k,r}(u),\qquad\forall u\in\mathcal{U}^{\mathrm{tr}}_{k,r},

for every k,rk,r, up to observational equivalence and regime relabeling.

For a model T^\hat{T} learned from finite data, we allow estimation and optimization error

ϵk,r:=supu∈𝒰k,rtr‖T^k,r​(u)−Tk,r​(u)‖2,\epsilon_{k,r}:=\sup_{u\in\mathcal{U}^{\mathrm{tr}}_{k,r}}\|\hat{T}_{k,r}(u)-T_{k,r}(u)\|_{2},

and assume ϵk,r→0\epsilon_{k,r}\rightarrow 0 as the amount of relevant training data grows and the training objective is optimized consistently.

J.2 Extrapolating Identified Mechanisms to Novel Compositions

Training-support identification does not by itself imply compositional generalization. Two mechanisms can agree on all observed training transitions and still disagree on a novel state–action composition induced by a goal shift. Recombination therefore requires additional structure that separates coordinates that affect a mechanism from coordinates that are only part of the global state.

Additive or separable functions provide one favorable case, which allow us to reuse the learned mechanisms for each factor zk,t+1z_{k,t+1}, but contact-rich world-model dynamics are often regime-dependent rather than purely additive. We propose a simpler scenario where each transition mechanisms Tk,rtT_{k,r_{t}} depends sparsely on the inputs st,ats_{t},a_{t}. For a fixed regime rr, let xt=(zt,at)x_{t}=(z_{t},a_{t}), then

zk,t+1=Tk,rt​(xt).z_{k,t+1}=T_{k,r_{t}}(x_{t}).

Sparsity of ∇xTk,rt​(x)\nabla_{x}T_{k,r_{t}}(x) implies that only a subset of coordinates affects the kk-th factor transition, while the remaining coordinates may change the global composition without changing this local mechanism.

Assumption 3 (Sparse local mechanisms)

For each factor kk and regime rr, there exists a fixed coordinate set Pk⊆{1,…,dim(x)}P_{k}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,\dim(x)\}, with |Pk|≪dim(x)|P_{k}|\ll\dim(x), such that

Tk,r​(x)=Tk,r​(xPk).T_{k,r}(x)=T_{k,r}(x_{P_{k}}).

Equivalently,

∂Tk,r​(x)∂xj=0∀j∉Pk.\frac{\partial T_{k,r}(x)}{\partial x_{j}}=0\qquad\forall j\notin P_{k}.

We write uk,t=xPk,tu_{k,t}=x_{P_{k},t} for the inputs relevant to the kk-th transition mechanism.

Sparse local mechanism can allow us to create favorable cases when a goal shift creates a novel global composition without creating novel local mechanism inputs.

Assumption 4 (Local support coverage)

Let

𝒰k,rte:=⋃t=0H−1supppte⁡(Uk,t∣Rt=r)\mathcal{U}_{k,r}^{\mathrm{te}}:=\bigcup_{t=0}^{H-1}\operatorname{supp}_{p_{\mathrm{te}}}(U_{k,t}\mid R_{t}=r)

denote the test support of the inputs of transition mechanism for factor kk. For every factor kk, assume

𝒰k,rte⊆𝒰k,rtr.\mathcal{U}_{k,r}^{\mathrm{te}}\subseteq\mathcal{U}_{k,r}^{\mathrm{tr}}.

Thus, the global state–action composition may be novel, but every local mechanism is queried only on local inputs covered during training.

Proposition 1 (Local active-coordinate coverage controls global error)

Let ℒtr​(T~)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{tr}}(\tilde{T}) denote the learning objective used to train the world model. Suppose that we perfectly optimize the world model on training support, then under assumption 1 and 2, we identify the learned model such that the true transition and learned transition share the same regime-conditioned local decomposition,

T⁡(zt,at)=(T1,rt​(uk,t),…,TK,rt​(uk,t)),T(z_{t},a_{t})=\bigl(T_{1,r_{t}}(u_{k,t}),\ldots,T_{K,r_{t}}(u_{k,t})\bigr),

and

T^​(zt,at)=(T^1,rt​(uk,t),…,T^K,rt​(uk,t)).\hat{T}(z_{t},a_{t})=\bigl(\hat{T}_{1,r_{t}}(u_{k,t}),\ldots,\hat{T}_{K,r_{t}}(u_{k,t})\bigr).

Assume that, for every factor kk and regime rr, we satisfy the assumption of sparse local mechanisms (assumption 3) and local support coverage (assumption 4).

Then, for any test composition (zt,at)∈𝒞te(z_{t},a_{t})\in\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{te}},

‖T^​(zt,at)−T⁡(zt,at)‖2≤(∑k=1Kϵk,rt2)1/2.\left\|\hat{T}(z_{t},a_{t})-T(z_{t},a_{t})\right\|_{2}\leq\left(\sum_{k=1}^{K}\epsilon_{k,r_{t}}^{2}\right)^{1/2}.

where

ϵk,r:=supu∈𝒰ktr‖T^k,r​(u)−Tk,r​(u)‖2.\epsilon_{k,r}:=\sup_{u\in\mathcal{U}_{k}^{\mathrm{tr}}}\left\|\hat{T}_{k,r}(u)-T_{k,r}(u)\right\|_{2}.

Consequently, if ϵk,r→0\epsilon_{k,r}\to 0 for all k,rk,r, then the world model generalizes to novel combinations present in the test support.

Proof.

Take any test composition (zt,at)∈𝒞te(z_{t},a_{t})\in\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{te}} with interaction regime rtr_{t}. By Assumption 4, for every factor kk,

uk,t∈𝒰k,rtte⊆𝒰k,rttr.u_{k,t}\in\mathcal{U}_{k,r_{t}}^{\mathrm{te}}\subseteq\mathcal{U}_{k,r_{t}}^{\mathrm{tr}}.

Thus, each local mechanism is evaluated within its regime-conditioned training support. By Assumption 2,

‖T^k,rt​(uk,t)−Tk,rt​(uk,t)‖2≤ϵk,rt.\left\|\hat{T}_{k,r_{t}}(u_{k,t})-T_{k,r_{t}}(u_{k,t})\right\|_{2}\leq\epsilon_{k,r_{t}}.

Since the true and learned transitions share the same factorized decomposition,

‖T^​(zt,at)−T⁡(zt,at)‖22\displaystyle\left\|\hat{T}(z_{t},a_{t})-T(z_{t},a_{t})\right\|_{2}^{2} =∑k=1K‖T^k,rt​(uk,t)−Tk,rt​(uk,t)‖22\displaystyle=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\left\|\hat{T}_{k,r_{t}}(u_{k,t})-T_{k,r_{t}}(u_{k,t})\right\|_{2}^{2}
≤∑k=1Kϵk,rt2.\displaystyle\leq\sum_{k=1}^{K}\epsilon_{k,r_{t}}^{2}.

Taking the square root completes the proof.

Discussion.

This construction should be read as an illustrative sufficient condition rather than a complete solution. Sparse local mechanisms reduce a high-dimensional global coverage problem to smaller local coverage problems, but they do not by themselves solve mechanism identification, regime discovery, or extrapolation to genuinely new local interactions. The broader challenge is to develop world-model architectures, objectives, and data-collection strategies that identify reusable action-conditioned mechanisms and impose enough structure on their interactions to support generalization beyond expert rollouts.

Appendix K AnyGoal Library and Reproducibility

We release AnyGoal as an open-source Python library for collecting goal-shifted datasets, training world models, and evaluating rollout prediction and MPC planning. The library provides both Python APIs and a unified CLI, allowing researchers to reproduce the benchmark experiments and evaluate additional models under the same protocol. AnyGoal builds on Stable-WorldModel (Maes et al., 2026a) and retains the original model implementations and numerical protocols. Complete installation instructions and API references are available in the online documentation.

K.1 Installation and Dataset Access

The library can be installed with evaluation dependencies using uv.

⬇
pip install uv
uv venv --python 3.10
source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install "anygoal[eval]"

The default installation provides dataset access, collection, validation, and simulation environments, while the eval and all extras add evaluation and training dependencies, respectively.

The CLI exposes a registry of supported datasets and models.

⬇
# Inspect available datasets and models
anygoal list datasets
anygoal list models
# Inspect default data and checkpoint paths
anygoal config path data
anygoal config path checkpoints

Datasets and pretrained checkpoints can be downloaded from Hugging Face through the artifact interface.

⬇
# Download training and test datasets
anygoal artifacts download --dataset pusht
anygoal artifacts download --dataset avoidt
# Download a pretrained model checkpoint
anygoal artifacts download --model lewm

Model integrations use the corresponding upstream implementations. Their source code can be installed separately.

⬇
anygoal models list
anygoal models install lewm
Dataset Collection

Beyond the released evaluation episodes, AnyGoal provides tools for generating additional goal-shifted trajectories. Dataset collection is available through both Python and CLI interfaces, which use the same in-package collectors.

The following example collects 400 Avoid-T episodes using eight parallel environments.

⬇
import anygoal
dataset = anygoal.collect(
"avoidt",
num_episodes=400,
num_parallel=8,
seed=0,
)

The equivalent collection procedure can be invoked from the terminal.

⬇
anygoal collect avoidt --num-episodes 400 --num-parallel 8
# Collect another goal-shifted variant
anygoal collect cubediagonal --output /path/to/cubediagonal.h5

K.2 World-Model Evaluation

AnyGoal provides standardized interfaces for evaluating a base-trained world model on both its original task and goal-shifted variants. The same model checkpoint can be used for rollout prediction and downstream MPC planning, enabling comparisons across evaluation metrics.

Planning evaluation.

The following commands evaluate LeWM on Push-T and Avoid-T.

⬇
# Original training goal
anygoal eval planning --model lewm --dataset pusht --seed 0
# Unseen goal
anygoal eval planning --model lewm --dataset avoidt --seed 0
Rollout evaluation.

The corresponding rollout-prediction evaluation uses the same model and dataset identifiers.

⬇
anygoal eval rollout --model lewm --dataset pusht --seed 0
anygoal eval rollout --model lewm --dataset avoidt --seed 0

By default, the evaluation commands resolve the checkpoint associated with the selected model and base-task family through the shared artifact catalog. Users can also specify a checkpoint explicitly with --checkpoint or download missing artifacts with --download.

The evaluation interfaces additionally support explicit random seeds, allowing comparisons across repeated runs.

K.3 Reproducibility and Extensibility

AnyGoal organizes datasets, checkpoints, and supported model implementations through shared registries. Dataset and model identifiers, artifact locations, and evaluation configurations can be specified explicitly, reducing ambiguity when reproducing experiments. The library exposes its core functionality through Python APIs, including anygoal.collect, anygoal.train, anygoal.evaluate_rollout, and anygoal.plan. These interfaces complement the CLI and support integration into existing research workflows.

The released benchmark contains 400 episodes per goal-shifted variant, while the collection tools allow researchers to construct additional evaluation datasets. Together with the standardized evaluation interfaces, this enables future world models to be tested on the same controlled goal shifts without reproducing the environment and evaluation infrastructure. The source code, configuration files, and implementation instructions are available at github.com/galilai-group/AnyGoal.
